name: Trayo API
description:
**Permissions:** each authenticated REST operation publishes `x-trayo-scope-requirements`
and a readable summary of its required permissions. MCP checks permissions per tool;
read each tool’s `_meta["trayo/scopeRequirements"]`. Read `GET /v1/whoami` for your
key’s configured scopes, current effective permissions and restrictions.
Request validation, workspace access rules and plan eligibility still apply.

Define accounts (companies) and signals (what you want to detect), run
discovery on demand, read the events discovery produces.

**Start with `GET /v1/whoami`.** It confirms the key and returns the
workspace, the plan, `canInitiate` and the lookup
limits — the numbers to plan against before you start. Then pick
a **recipe**: the call sequences that make up a task (track companies and
read events; find lookalike companies; find and keep prospects; stakeholders at a company with
contact details; a brief before outreach; recent movers) are published at
`GET /v1/recipes`, carried in this document as `x-recipes`, and rendered
in `/llms.txt`. Each step names the operation, what it does in that
sequence, and for a poll step the condition that ends the loop. Every
operation below also carries `x-codeSamples` — a `curl` and a Python
sample generated from its own parameters and request schema.

Create or reuse accounts and signals. Then call `POST /v1/discoveries` with the account IDs, signal keys, and lookback window.
Add `people: "add"` when you want the people who matter to each event added and listed on it; by default a run adds no people.

**Give a new account the strongest identity you have.** Send its bare
`linkedinHandle` whenever you know the LinkedIn company page; it is checked
before the website `url`, then the name. A correct handle at create time
makes a `company_not_found` result less likely.

**Discovery is ASYNCHRONOUS.** The POST returns 202 immediately with a run
whose `status` is `running` — it has not searched anything yet. Poll
`GET /v1/discoveries/{runId}` until `settledAt` is non-null, then read
the events standing for its scope with `GET /v1/events?discoveryRunId={runId}`.
That scope is everything the run wrote — at any event date, because a job
change is dated by the month the job STARTED and can predate the lookback —
plus the canonical events matching the run's accounts, signals and lookback
window, including ones earlier runs wrote. Paged to the end, a settled run
therefore yields at least `eventsNew` events — one page is capped and need
not, so follow `nextCursor` before comparing anything to that counter.
Reading it before `settledAt` returns what the run has written so far.

**Run your signals together, not one at a time.** Every event carries
`signalKeys`, the keys of the signals that matched it, so a single run over
many signals stays attributable event by event. Do not split a run per
signal to find out which one fired. `signalType` will not tell you — it is
the kind of source a signal reads (`news`, `jobs`, `job_change`) and your
signals share a handful of those between them.

**`settledAt` is the finish line.** A run has two halves — searching your
accounts, then writing what the search found as events — and it is final
only when both are done. `settledAt` is set at that instant, `status` reads
`completed` or `failed` at the same instant, and from then on the candidate
and event counts are frozen: they are the run's receipt and stay what they
were even if you later delete some of the events it created.

`completedAt` marks only the first half, the search. It can be set while
`status` is still `running`, because the events from that search are still
being written. **Do not poll on `completedAt`, and do not try to detect the
end by watching `eventsNew` stop changing** — a pause between two writes
looks exactly like the end of a run and is not one. Wait for `settledAt`.

`status` is the POLLING signal: it tells you when to stop calling, nothing
more. `candidatesScreened`, `candidatesMatched` and `eventsNew` are the RUN
RECEIPT — what this execution screened, what matched a signal, and what it
wrote — not the size of the scoped events page. Candidates are not events:
`candidatesScreened: 12` with `candidatesMatched: 0` means nothing matched,
and `bySignal` gives both counts per signal, so a signal that matched nothing
shows 0. `eventsFound` is the deprecated name for `candidatesScreened`. Read the page,
`error`, and `blockedSignals`; even a `completed` run with a non-null `error`
ended without doing everything it was asked to.

**A run also says what it could NOT search.** `blockedSignals`, on the 202
and on every poll, names each ready signal that cannot produce results for
part of the run, why, and — in `accountIds` — WHICH accounts. Read it before
concluding from `eventsNew: 0` that there was nothing to find: an account
that was not searched is indistinguishable from a real empty result on the
counts alone.

You can use a new signal key in discovery immediately.
These outcomes apply to every signal type, including `news`. While a run is active, keep polling the same run. `account_not_ready` means Trayo could not search the account this time. After the run settles, retry the affected account IDs. `company_not_found` means Trayo could not identify the company from the supplied details. For `company_not_found`, check the named accounts before starting another discovery. If an identity is wrong, send the correct `linkedinHandle` with `trayo_update_account` over MCP, or with `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` and a workspace API key over REST. When no handle is known, send a corrected website `url` instead. Both need `accounts:write`. `trayo_update_account` also reports whether Trayo can now identify the company. Importing the same hostname again skips the existing account and does not update it. After the current run settles, start a new discovery for the corrected account IDs.

**Re-running an identical discovery is safe.** Results are deduplicated
against everything already in the workspace, so calling the same
accounts/signals/lookback again typically returns `eventsNew: 0` and creates
no duplicate events. The `discoveryRunId` event read still returns the
matching events that already stand for that scope. Zero is SUCCESS, not
failure, and not a reason to retry. A retry loop that treats `eventsNew: 0`
as an error will never terminate.

**Errors** are always `{ "error": { type, code, retry, message, param,
requestId } }`. `code` identifies the reason from the documented set.
Every failure includes a code, including request validation failures.
`retry` tells you what to DO about it without parsing the message:
`fix_input` (change the request), `retry_later` (send the same request again
shortly, with backoff and a FINITE number of attempts), `do_not_retry` (it
will never work). Branch on `code`; fall back to `retry` when you only need
to decide whether to send the request again, or when you meet a `code` you
do not recognise — that fallback is what lets a client written today keep
working against an error added tomorrow. The full table, with every code's
status and retry class, is in the `Error` schema.

Two 409s make the point: `idempotency_in_progress` and
`idempotency_key_reused` share a status and demand OPPOSITE responses —
repeat the identical request with the same key, versus never send that
request again unchanged. Never infer recovery from the HTTP status.

**Rate limits.** Every route shares the workspace budget, in two buckets, each a
rolling 60-second window. A workspace starts with 120
requests per minute for the API and a separate
7 per minute for the routes
that do the most work per call, `POST /v1/discoveries`, `POST /v1/find`, `POST /v1/accounts/lookalikes`, `POST /v1/companies/competitors`, `POST /v1/posts/search`, `POST /v1/posts/search/keywords`, `POST /v1/research/person/batch`, `POST /v1/stakeholders/search/batch` and `POST /v1/people/enrich/batch`; a call spends one
bucket or the other, never both, and each MCP tool names the bucket it spends in its description and
`_meta["trayo/rateLimitBucket"]`. REST, MCP, all API keys and OAuth users share
the same workspace buckets; adding credentials does not increase throughput.
Support can adjust these defaults for a workspace, so read your budget rather than
hardcoding these numbers: EVERY authenticated response, successful ones included, carries
`RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` (seconds
until the window frees up) for the bucket that request was counted in. That
is how you slow down BEFORE being refused. Over the limit is
`429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After` in seconds: wait that long, then send
the same request again.

**Fanning out is what actually hits this** — a hundred concurrent
calls to any route are a hundred requests in one window, not one — and
**`GET /v1/whoami` is limited like everything else**, so a
balance poll on a timer spends the same budget as the work it is watching.
Back the poll off with the rest of your client, or drop it: the
`RateLimit-*` headers on the responses you are already getting say more,
sooner, for nothing. A per-network limit also sits in front of every `/v1`
route, before the key is read: a burst from one network can be refused
there, and that 429 carries `Retry-After` and no `RateLimit-*`. It is the
only limit on the unauthenticated document routes under `/v1` — fetch the
document once and reuse it.

**Usage limits.** Public REST and MCP usage quotas and daily usage caps are
disabled for now. Lookup allowances report `null` in `GET /v1/whoami`
(MCP: `trayo_whoami`). Usage is still recorded; workspace request pacing still applies.
Authentication, permissions, workspace lifecycle and request validation still apply.

**Pagination.** Six list routes — `GET /v1/accounts`, `GET /v1/people`,
`GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/discoveries`, `GET /v1/lists`,
`GET /v1/lists/{id}/members` — return `{ data, hasMore,
nextCursor }`; follow `nextCursor` until `hasMore` is false.
`POST /v1/find` also paginates when you send only `filters`: repeat the
same request with `nextCursor` as `cursor`, preserving the filters, until
`hasMore` is false. Any search with a `query`, including one that also
sends `filters`, returns one ranked page and rejects a `cursor`.
`GET /v1/signals`, `POST /v1/stakeholders/search` and the research routes
do not paginate. `GET /v1/signals` carries the list envelope with
`hasMore` always false. `POST /v1/job-changes/search` pages with its own
`limit`/`cursor`/`nextCursor` on the body, not on the query string, and
only when you send `destination`.

**Naming across routes:** two things go by different names depending on
the route, and nothing is renamed for you — map them at your boundary.
The **company website** is `url` on an account, `domain` on the `company`
block of `POST /v1/people`, and `website` on the routes that take a company
reference (`POST /v1/research/company`, `POST /v1/stakeholders/search`,
`POST /v1/job-changes/search`, `POST /v1/contacts/lookup`); a
`POST /v1/find` accounts row carries both `domain` and `url`. The
**LinkedIn page** is a bare handle in an account's `linkedinHandle` and in
a person's own `linkedinUsername`, and a full URL in `linkedinUrl` on the
company references and on find results. Different names, the same company
website and the same LinkedIn page.

**Prospecting:** `POST /v1/find` searches for companies and people.
For direct stored-data search, send `mode: "direct"` with exact `filters`
and a limit up to 100. For people, company filters select their current
employer and `filters.title` selects the person; each row includes both.
Direct mode does not accept a sentence query or automatically expand criteria.
A company without a website is still returned; use its ID for follow-up searches.
Check `truncated` and `notes`; per-company limits can leave additional people unseen.
`POST /v1/posts/search/keywords` directly searches stored LinkedIn posts:
`concepts` is an AND of groups, each containing OR phrase alternatives.
This supports explicit query decomposition and synonym expansion in one call.
Its results rank keyword relevance within a bounded sample of 200 ranked candidates, with coverage even when empty.
It searches at most seven days of the recent-post index (bodies of at least 120 characters).
Retrieval is always non-exhaustive; an empty result cannot prove absence.
Direct searches use an eight-second request budget and shared capacity limits.
On `data_search_busy`, wait for `details.retryAfterSeconds`; on
`data_search_timeout`, narrow the criteria. Neither error means no matches.
`POST /v1/accounts/lookalikes` finds companies similar to supplied seeds.
Both return candidates without saving them — you post selected results
back to `/v1/accounts/batch` or `/v1/people/batch` to bring them in.
`POST /v1/companies/competitors` ranks the competitors of one company.
Find with a sentence query draws on your search quota per search that runs; contact lookups (below)
draw on your plan's lookup allowance. Research, stakeholder search and
asking about a person draw on the same usage quota per answer returned.
Nothing else in this API is metered.

**Working sets:** `/v1/lists` is where the set of people or accounts you
are acting on lives between calls. Create one, add members by `personId`
or `accountId` with a `via` that records how they got there (`find`,
`signal`, `import`, `manual`), then hand the LIST — not your session — to
whatever acts on it: a CRM push, a campaign, a human. Adding a member who is
already there is a skip, not an error, so the same batch is safe to send
twice. Lists are scoped to the user your key acts as, and show up in the
Trayo app under that user. Do not mark a working set with `starred`, a
person's `note`, or a marker in `title` — that is what lists are for.

**Ranking:** every account carries `scores` — Trayo's own view of how
much is happening there — so you do not have to rebuild a ranking by
counting events. `scores.timing.score` (0–100, normalized against your
workspace's hottest account, as the product defines it) is the number for
"who is worth working this week"; `scores.timing.raw` is the un-normalized
value that holds still for absolute thresholds;
`scores.activity` adds the event count, average significance and relevance,
and a generated prose `summary` of what the events add up to. Both are
null until Trayo has scored the account, and nothing in this API
triggers scoring. `GET /v1/accounts` does not sort by them yet: page
through and sort client-side.

**Contact enrichment:** `POST /v1/people/{id}/enrich` finds a person's
email and/or phone the same way the Trayo app's own "Find email" does,
and `POST /v1/people/enrich/batch` accepts up to 200 ids per call. Its
45-second budget for starting lookups is checked once, before anything is
reserved; the whole batch starts together in a few seconds. The batch answers `200`
with partial results. Retain the submitted ids: `skipped[].index` maps to
that request. Re-send rows skipped because time ran out in smaller batches;
nothing was started or charged for them. Other skip reasons, including
allowance refusals and invalid ids, require their own remedy. Single-person
lookup requests answer `202`; both routes use `GET /v1/people/{id}/enrich` to poll.
These lookups are
explicit (nothing is looked up on create or read), asynchronous, idempotent
(re-sending never double-runs or is charged twice — a field already
running, already found, blocked by an email you wrote, or inside its retry
cooldown is reported in `skipped`, not raised), and governed by your plan:
each lookup counts against the
plan's lookup limit (`402 lookup_limit_reached` before anything runs).
Every found value carries
`source`, `status` and `foundAt`; a value you wrote is `source: "manual"`
and is never overwritten by a found one.

**Workspace settings:** `PATCH /v1/workspace` sets your stakeholder
definition — plain prose describing who buys and owns what you sell, and
who to skip — plus `solutions` and `solutionsBrief`, what you sell. The
definition steers stakeholder search and the per-event people (with
`reasoning`) that a discovery run started with `people: "add"` attaches;
the default, `people: "none"`, attaches none. Without it stakeholder search seeds
on seniority alone and no people are attached to events. **Set it FIRST,
before you run discovery** — it applies to work
that starts after it is set, not retroactively. The definition is carried as
`stakeholderCriteria` on the workspace and as `definition` on stakeholder
search.

**Stakeholders:** `POST /v1/stakeholders/search` takes a company — any
company by its website, or an account of yours — and a stakeholder definition,
and returns the people at it who fit, best first, each with a reason.
Synchronous, seconds, read-only: nothing is written, import the ones you
want with `POST /v1/people/batch`. It is the product's own stakeholder
finding (definition → keywords → candidate search → selection) without the
persistence, so it works for a company you have never touched. Omit the
definition to use the workspace's; the response says which applied.
Each person carries `matchedPersona` and each company `coverage` (every
persona, and whether anyone matched it); each label is checked against the
job's function and seniority. When nobody fits, `nearMisses` holds the
closest candidates flagged `belowThreshold: true`. Repeating a search
within a week normally returns the same people. For many companies,
`POST /v1/stakeholders/search/batch` takes up to 50 in one call and searches
them ten at a time, reporting each in `results` or `errors` by `index`.

**Recent moves:** `POST /v1/job-changes/search` finds people who changed
company. Send `source` (the company left), `destination` (the company
joined), or both. Without a company, send `title` (the new role, same
terms as `/v1/find` `filters.title`), optionally with `destinationFilters`
(`hq.countries`, `headcount` of the company joined). Inclusive `startedSince` and
exclusive `startedBefore` bound the start month for either kind of search. `startedSince` (the
month the new role started) narrows either kind of search: "who became
CISO since August at US companies over 500 people" is one call, and so is
"who joined Stripe as an executive since September". It returns moves
observed in the last 90 days — the person, the two companies, the title on
each side, when the move was detected, and when the new role started to the
month — and writes nothing. One row per person per destination.
`limit` sets the page size: 25 by default, 100 at most, capped rather than
rejected. `hasMore` says more matches may remain behind this page; send
`nextCursor` back as `cursor`, verbatim and with the same search, to walk
them. The walk resumes where the page stopped, so a later page neither
repeats nor skips what an earlier one returned. `hasMore` reads the row
count before duplicate records are collapsed, so a page can come back
short and still be `true` — follow `hasMore` and `nextCursor`, never the
row count. A source-only search may read a fixed sample rather than an ordered
walk: only that sampled search cannot page, and sending a cursor is rejected.
Indexed source-only searches accept cursors. For a sampled source-only search,
`nextCursor` is null, and `hasMore: true` means narrow the
search. Report truncation
for the requested period. `detectedSince` filters detection recency: only moves with
`detectedAt >=` the value you send — the date the move was DETECTED, not the
date the role started, which startedSince and startedBefore filter. It only narrows the 90-day
window, starting at midnight UTC 90 days ago: an earlier value is clamped to
that start and a future value matches nothing. Destination searches already return
the newest moves first: narrowing the window does not recover omitted matches;
it returns the same rows or a subset. This is a recency filter, not pagination.
`seniority` is the second filter: it keeps only moves INTO a role at that
level or above, read from the title of the role they joined — not the one
they left, and not a title list you supply. The four seniority levels widen
in order: `cxo` (the C-suite), `vp` (adds VP, SVP, EVP, Vice President and
President), `director` (adds Director), `head` (adds Partner, Principal and
Head of). With `destination`, it WIDENS the search rather than trimming the page — the search
reads further through recent moves looking for matches instead of filtering
the slice it would have read without it — and that wider read is still
bounded, so a short or empty answer does not prove nobody senior joined.
Source-only searches that report `sampled: true` filter the same fixed sample; they do not read further. Title matching is heuristic and excludes assistant/support roles.
`sampled: true` means a source-only search read a small
fixed sample of recent moves: an empty answer does not mean nobody left,
and retrying gives the same answer while the underlying data is unchanged.
A source-only search with `sampled: false` walked the newest moves out of
that company instead of sampling them.
With `destination`, `sampled` is false: the search reads a bounded slice of
the newest moves into that company before filtering by source.
`hasMore: false` does not prove completeness with either value of `sampled`.
Every row is a move between two companies; promotions and same-company
title changes never appear here. For hires and promotions at a watched
company, use the workspace `job_change` signal (`create_signal`, then
`run_discovery`). That signal is not a departure search and does not provide
a complete list of who left. Import the people you want with
`POST /v1/people/batch`.

**Research:** `POST /v1/research/company` and `POST /v1/research/person`
return the quick overview the Trayo app opens its drawer with — for a
company: what it does, `whyNow` hooks from its recent updates, and `fit`
against what you sell; for a person: career, likely challenges, and the
angles that tie their role to what you sell. Synchronous, stateless,
read-only: one read of Trayo's own data, one generated answer, nothing stored,
nothing written, any company or person we hold — not only the ones in your
workspace. Both read your `solutions` and stakeholder definition from the
workspace for the seller side of the answer.

`POST /v1/research/person/batch` is the person route for up to
10 people in one call, always ungrounded, reading your seller
context once for the whole batch. A person it cannot resolve or answer for
is reported in `errors` by its `index`, with the same `code` and `retry` an
error response carries, so one bad profile never costs you the rest of the
batch. An overview that came back empty is one of those errors
(`person_profile_too_thin`), never a blank result.

**Contact lookup without a person:** `POST /v1/contacts/lookup` takes a name
plus a LinkedIn profile or a company website and returns that person's email
in the same response, for somebody who is not in your workspace and does not
have to be. Ask for `fields: ["phone"]` and it answers `202` with a
`lookupId` to collect from `GET /v1/contacts/lookups/{lookupId}` — the phone
lookup can take several minutes. One lookup per
field, against your plan's allowance for that field — email and phone have
separate limits, and a lookup here draws on the same allowance as a lookup
on a person. Asking again for the same person reads the stored answer for
nothing.

**Ask about a person:** `POST /v1/people/{id}/ask` answers one question
about one person in your workspace from everything on record — the Trayo
record (contact details, the account and its research, the signals the
person is attached to and why, the sequences and emails sent with their
outcomes, lists, notes) plus the LinkedIn profile Trayo holds for them
(work history, recent posts). Send an `intent` — what you will do with the
answer — to steer focus and form. Synchronous, seconds, read-only,
grounded in that dossier only: nothing is searched, nothing is guessed,
and `sources` is a receipt of what Trayo read. Each answer draws on
your usage quota.

**Which of the two to ask.** `POST /v1/research/person` is a FIXED overview
of ANY person Trayo holds, built from their public profile — use it for
someone you have just found and do not have. `POST /v1/people/{id}/ask`
takes YOUR question about a person you already hold, and is the only route
that can see your own history with them: what discovery attached to them,
what you sent, whether they replied. "Who is this person" is research;
"did we ever email her, and is she worth a sequence" is ask.

**Limits go two ways, on purpose.** `POST /v1/find`'s `limit` CLAMPS at 50.
A `/v1/…/batch` array over its cap is an ERROR — 200 items on the write
batches, 10 on `POST /v1/research/person/batch`. Silently dropping
batch rows would lose records you believe you created; rejecting an over-large
find `limit` would draw on your search quota for a number you could have read
here.

**Auth:** every route below requires `Authorization: Bearer <key>` except
a few unauthenticated discovery routes, so a caller can find and read
this document before it has a key configured: `GET /` and `GET /v1` return
a small JSON index naming the document and how to authenticate, and this
document itself is served at `GET /openapi.json`,
`GET /.well-known/openapi` and `GET /v1/openapi.yaml`. All three are the
SAME document; the extension picks the default serialization and an
`Accept` header of `application/json` or `application/yaml` overrides it.
The same reference as Markdown is at `GET /llms.txt` (a short index) and
`GET /llms-full.txt` (everything, in one file); `GET /v1/recipes` is
unauthenticated too.

`error`, and `blockedSignals`; even a `completed` run with a non-null `error`
ended without doing everything it was asked to.

**A run also says what it could NOT search.** `blockedSignals`, on the 202
and on every poll, names each ready signal that cannot produce results for
part of the run, why, and — in `accountIds` — WHICH accounts. Read it before
concluding from `eventsNew: 0` that there was nothing to find: an account
that was not searched is indistinguishable from a real empty result on the
counts alone.

You can use a new signal key in discovery immediately.
These outcomes apply to every signal type, including `news`. While a run is active, keep polling the same run. `account_not_ready` means Trayo could not search the account this time. After the run settles, retry the affected account IDs. `company_not_found` means Trayo could not identify the company from the supplied details. For `company_not_found`, check the named accounts before starting another discovery. If an identity is wrong, send the correct `linkedinHandle` with `trayo_update_account` over MCP, or with `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` and a workspace API key over REST. When no handle is known, send a corrected website `url` instead. Both need `accounts:write`. `trayo_update_account` also reports whether Trayo can now identify the company. Importing the same hostname again skips the existing account and does not update it. After the current run settles, start a new discovery for the corrected account IDs.

**Re-running an identical discovery is safe.** Results are deduplicated
against everything already in the workspace, so calling the same
accounts/signals/lookback again typically returns `eventsNew: 0` and creates
no duplicate events. The `discoveryRunId` event read still returns the
matching events that already stand for that scope. Zero is SUCCESS, not
failure, and not a reason to retry. A retry loop that treats `eventsNew: 0`
as an error will never terminate.

**Errors** are always `{ "error": { type, code, retry, message, param,
requestId } }`. `code` identifies the reason from the documented set.
Every failure includes a code, including request validation failures.
`retry` tells you what to DO about it without parsing the message:
`fix_input` (change the request), `retry_later` (send the same request again
shortly, with backoff and a FINITE number of attempts), `do_not_retry` (it
will never work). Branch on `code`; fall back to `retry` when you only need
to decide whether to send the request again, or when you meet a `code` you
do not recognise — that fallback is what lets a client written today keep
working against an error added tomorrow. The full table, with every code's
status and retry class, is in the `Error` schema.

Two 409s make the point: `idempotency_in_progress` and
`idempotency_key_reused` share a status and demand OPPOSITE responses —
repeat the identical request with the same key, versus never send that
request again unchanged. Never infer recovery from the HTTP status.

**Rate limits.** Every route shares the workspace budget, in two buckets, each a
rolling 60-second window. A workspace starts with 120
requests per minute for the API and a separate
7 per minute for the routes
that do the most work per call, `POST /v1/discoveries`, `POST /v1/find`, `POST /v1/accounts/lookalikes`, `POST /v1/companies/competitors`, `POST /v1/posts/search`, `POST /v1/posts/search/keywords`, `POST /v1/research/person/batch`, `POST /v1/stakeholders/search/batch` and `POST /v1/people/enrich/batch`; a call spends one
bucket or the other, never both, and each MCP tool names the bucket it spends in its description and
`_meta["trayo/rateLimitBucket"]`. REST, MCP, all API keys and OAuth users share
the same workspace buckets; adding credentials does not increase throughput.
Support can adjust these defaults for a workspace, so read your budget rather than
hardcoding these numbers: EVERY authenticated response, successful ones included, carries
`RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` (seconds
until the window frees up) for the bucket that request was counted in. That
is how you slow down BEFORE being refused. Over the limit is
`429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After` in seconds: wait that long, then send
the same request again.

**Fanning out is what actually hits this** — a hundred concurrent
calls to any route are a hundred requests in one window, not one — and
**`GET /v1/whoami` is limited like everything else**, so a
balance poll on a timer spends the same budget as the work it is watching.
Back the poll off with the rest of your client, or drop it: the
`RateLimit-*` headers on the responses you are already getting say more,
sooner, for nothing. A per-network limit also sits in front of every `/v1`
route, before the key is read: a burst from one network can be refused
there, and that 429 carries `Retry-After` and no `RateLimit-*`. It is the
only limit on the unauthenticated document routes under `/v1` — fetch the
document once and reuse it.

**Usage limits.** Public REST and MCP usage quotas and daily usage caps are
disabled for now. Lookup allowances report `null` in `GET /v1/whoami`
(MCP: `trayo_whoami`). Usage is still recorded; workspace request pacing still applies.
Authentication, permissions, workspace lifecycle and request validation still apply.

**Pagination.** Six list routes — `GET /v1/accounts`, `GET /v1/people`,
`GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/discoveries`, `GET /v1/lists`,
`GET /v1/lists/{id}/members` — return `{ data, hasMore,
nextCursor }`; follow `nextCursor` until `hasMore` is false.
`POST /v1/find` also paginates when you send only `filters`: repeat the
same request with `nextCursor` as `cursor`, preserving the filters, until
`hasMore` is false. Any search with a `query`, including one that also
sends `filters`, returns one ranked page and rejects a `cursor`.
`GET /v1/signals`, `POST /v1/stakeholders/search` and the research routes
do not paginate. `GET /v1/signals` carries the list envelope with
`hasMore` always false. `POST /v1/job-changes/search` pages with its own
`limit`/`cursor`/`nextCursor` on the body, not on the query string, and
only when you send `destination`.

**Naming across routes:** two things go by different names depending on
the route, and nothing is renamed for you — map them at your boundary.
The **company website** is `url` on an account, `domain` on the `company`
block of `POST /v1/people`, and `website` on the routes that take a company
reference (`POST /v1/research/company`, `POST /v1/stakeholders/search`,
`POST /v1/job-changes/search`, `POST /v1/contacts/lookup`); a
`POST /v1/find` accounts row carries both `domain` and `url`. The
**LinkedIn page** is a bare handle in an account's `linkedinHandle` and in
a person's own `linkedinUsername`, and a full URL in `linkedinUrl` on the
company references and on find results. Different names, the same company
website and the same LinkedIn page.

**Prospecting:** `POST /v1/find` searches for companies and people.
For direct stored-data search, send `mode: "direct"` with exact `filters`
and a limit up to 100. For people, company filters select their current
employer and `filters.title` selects the person; each row includes both.
Direct mode does not accept a sentence query or automatically expand criteria.
A company without a website is still returned; use its ID for follow-up searches.
Check `truncated` and `notes`; per-company limits can leave additional people unseen.
`POST /v1/posts/search/keywords` directly searches stored LinkedIn posts:
`concepts` is an AND of groups, each containing OR phrase alternatives.
This supports explicit query decomposition and synonym expansion in one call.
Its results rank keyword relevance within a bounded sample of 200 ranked candidates, with coverage even when empty.
It searches at most seven days of the recent-post index (bodies of at least 120 characters).
Retrieval is always non-exhaustive; an empty result cannot prove absence.
Direct searches use an eight-second request budget and shared capacity limits.
On `data_search_busy`, wait for `details.retryAfterSeconds`; on
`data_search_timeout`, narrow the criteria. Neither error means no matches.
`POST /v1/accounts/lookalikes` finds companies similar to supplied seeds.
Both return candidates without saving them — you post selected results
back to `/v1/accounts/batch` or `/v1/people/batch` to bring them in.
`POST /v1/companies/competitors` ranks the competitors of one company.
Find with a sentence query draws on your search quota per search that runs; contact lookups (below)
draw on your plan's lookup allowance. Research, stakeholder search and
asking about a person draw on the same usage quota per answer returned.
Nothing else in this API is metered.

**Working sets:** `/v1/lists` is where the set of people or accounts you
are acting on lives between calls. Create one, add members by `personId`
or `accountId` with a `via` that records how they got there (`find`,
`signal`, `import`, `manual`), then hand the LIST — not your session — to
whatever acts on it: a CRM push, a campaign, a human. Adding a member who is
already there is a skip, not an error, so the same batch is safe to send
twice. Lists are scoped to the user your key acts as, and show up in the
Trayo app under that user. Do not mark a working set with `starred`, a
person's `note`, or a marker in `title` — that is what lists are for.

**Ranking:** every account carries `scores` — Trayo's own view of how
much is happening there — so you do not have to rebuild a ranking by
counting events. `scores.timing.score` (0–100, normalized against your
workspace's hottest account, as the product defines it) is the number for
"who is worth working this week"; `scores.timing.raw` is the un-normalized
value that holds still for absolute thresholds;
`scores.activity` adds the event count, average significance and relevance,
and a generated prose `summary` of what the events add up to. Both are
null until Trayo has scored the account, and nothing in this API
triggers scoring. `GET /v1/accounts` does not sort by them yet: page
through and sort client-side.

**Contact enrichment:** `POST /v1/people/{id}/enrich` finds a person's
email and/or phone the same way the Trayo app's own "Find email" does,
and `POST /v1/people/enrich/batch` accepts up to 200 ids per call. Its
45-second budget for starting lookups is checked once, before anything is
reserved; the whole batch starts together in a few seconds. The batch answers `200`
with partial results. Retain the submitted ids: `skipped[].index` maps to
that request. Re-send rows skipped because time ran out in smaller batches;
nothing was started or charged for them. Other skip reasons, including
allowance refusals and invalid ids, require their own remedy. Single-person
lookup requests answer `202`; both routes use `GET /v1/people/{id}/enrich` to poll.
These lookups are
explicit (nothing is looked up on create or read), asynchronous, idempotent
(re-sending never double-runs or is charged twice — a field already
running, already found, blocked by an email you wrote, or inside its retry
cooldown is reported in `skipped`, not raised), and governed by your plan:
each lookup counts against the
plan's lookup limit (`402 lookup_limit_reached` before anything runs).
Every found value carries
`source`, `status` and `foundAt`; a value you wrote is `source: "manual"`
and is never overwritten by a found one.

**Workspace settings:** `PATCH /v1/workspace` sets your stakeholder
definition — plain prose describing who buys and owns what you sell, and
who to skip — plus `solutions` and `solutionsBrief`, what you sell. The
definition steers stakeholder search and the per-event people (with
`reasoning`) that a discovery run started with `people: "add"` attaches;
the default, `people: "none"`, attaches none. Without it stakeholder search seeds
on seniority alone and no people are attached to events. **Set it FIRST,
before you run discovery** — it applies to work
that starts after it is set, not retroactively. The definition is carried as
`stakeholderCriteria` on the workspace and as `definition` on stakeholder
search.

**Stakeholders:** `POST /v1/stakeholders/search` takes a company — any
company by its website, or an account of yours — and a stakeholder definition,
and returns the people at it who fit, best first, each with a reason.
Synchronous, seconds, read-only: nothing is written, import the ones you
want with `POST /v1/people/batch`. It is the product's own stakeholder
finding (definition → keywords → candidate search → selection) without the
persistence, so it works for a company you have never touched. Omit the
definition to use the workspace's; the response says which applied.
Each person carries `matchedPersona` and each company `coverage` (every
persona, and whether anyone matched it); each label is checked against the
job's function and seniority. When nobody fits, `nearMisses` holds the
closest candidates flagged `belowThreshold: true`. Repeating a search
within a week normally returns the same people. For many companies,
`POST /v1/stakeholders/search/batch` takes up to 50 in one call and searches
them ten at a time, reporting each in `results` or `errors` by `index`.

**Recent moves:** `POST /v1/job-changes/search` finds people who changed
company. Send `source` (the company left), `destination` (the company
joined), or both. Without a company, send `title` (the new role, same
terms as `/v1/find` `filters.title`), optionally with `destinationFilters`
(`hq.countries`, `headcount` of the company joined). Inclusive `startedSince` and
exclusive `startedBefore` bound the start month for either kind of search. `startedSince` (the
month the new role started) narrows either kind of search: "who became
CISO since August at US companies over 500 people" is one call, and so is
"who joined Stripe as an executive since September". It returns moves
observed in the last 90 days — the person, the two companies, the title on
each side, when the move was detected, and when the new role started to the
month — and writes nothing. One row per person per destination.
`limit` sets the page size: 25 by default, 100 at most, capped rather than
rejected. `hasMore` says more matches may remain behind this page; send
`nextCursor` back as `cursor`, verbatim and with the same search, to walk
them. The walk resumes where the page stopped, so a later page neither
repeats nor skips what an earlier one returned. `hasMore` reads the row
count before duplicate records are collapsed, so a page can come back
short and still be `true` — follow `hasMore` and `nextCursor`, never the
row count. A source-only search may read a fixed sample rather than an ordered
walk: only that sampled search cannot page, and sending a cursor is rejected.
Indexed source-only searches accept cursors. For a sampled source-only search,
`nextCursor` is null, and `hasMore: true` means narrow the
search. Report truncation
for the requested period. `detectedSince` filters detection recency: only moves with
`detectedAt >=` the value you send — the date the move was DETECTED, not the
date the role started, which startedSince and startedBefore filter. It only narrows the 90-day
window, starting at midnight UTC 90 days ago: an earlier value is clamped to
that start and a future value matches nothing. Destination searches already return
the newest moves first: narrowing the window does not recover omitted matches;
it returns the same rows or a subset. This is a recency filter, not pagination.
`seniority` is the second filter: it keeps only moves INTO a role at that
level or above, read from the title of the role they joined — not the one
they left, and not a title list you supply. The four seniority levels widen
in order: `cxo` (the C-suite), `vp` (adds VP, SVP, EVP, Vice President and
President), `director` (adds Director), `head` (adds Partner, Principal and
Head of). With `destination`, it WIDENS the search rather than trimming the page — the search
reads further through recent moves looking for matches instead of filtering
the slice it would have read without it — and that wider read is still
bounded, so a short or empty answer does not prove nobody senior joined.
Source-only searches that report `sampled: true` filter the same fixed sample; they do not read further. Title matching is heuristic and excludes assistant/support roles.
`sampled: true` means a source-only search read a small
fixed sample of recent moves: an empty answer does not mean nobody left,
and retrying gives the same answer while the underlying data is unchanged.
A source-only search with `sampled: false` walked the newest moves out of
that company instead of sampling them.
With `destination`, `sampled` is false: the search reads a bounded slice of
the newest moves into that company before filtering by source.
`hasMore: false` does not prove completeness with either value of `sampled`.
Every row is a move between two companies; promotions and same-company
title changes never appear here. For hires and promotions at a watched
company, use the workspace `job_change` signal (`create_signal`, then
`run_discovery`). That signal is not a departure search and does not provide
a complete list of who left. Import the people you want with
`POST /v1/people/batch`.

**Research:** `POST /v1/research/company` and `POST /v1/research/person`
return the quick overview the Trayo app opens its drawer with — for a
company: what it does, `whyNow` hooks from its recent updates, and `fit`
against what you sell; for a person: career, likely challenges, and the
angles that tie their role to what you sell. Synchronous, stateless,
read-only: one read of Trayo's own data, one generated answer, nothing stored,
nothing written, any company or person we hold — not only the ones in your
workspace. Both read your `solutions` and stakeholder definition from the
workspace for the seller side of the answer.

`POST /v1/research/person/batch` is the person route for up to
10 people in one call, always ungrounded, reading your seller
context once for the whole batch. A person it cannot resolve or answer for
is reported in `errors` by its `index`, with the same `code` and `retry` an
error response carries, so one bad profile never costs you the rest of the
batch. An overview that came back empty is one of those errors
(`person_profile_too_thin`), never a blank result.

**Contact lookup without a person:** `POST /v1/contacts/lookup` takes a name
plus a LinkedIn profile or a company website and returns that person's email
in the same response, for somebody who is not in your workspace and does not
have to be. Ask for `fields: ["phone"]` and it answers `202` with a
`lookupId` to collect from `GET /v1/contacts/lookups/{lookupId}` — the phone
lookup can take several minutes. One lookup per
field, against your plan's allowance for that field — email and phone have
separate limits, and a lookup here draws on the same allowance as a lookup
on a person. Asking again for the same person reads the stored answer for
nothing.

**Ask about a person:** `POST /v1/people/{id}/ask` answers one question
about one person in your workspace from everything on record — the Trayo
record (contact details, the account and its research, the signals the
person is attached to and why, the sequences and emails sent with their
outcomes, lists, notes) plus the LinkedIn profile Trayo holds for them
(work history, recent posts). Send an `intent` — what you will do with the
answer — to steer focus and form. Synchronous, seconds, read-only,
grounded in that dossier only: nothing is searched, nothing is guessed,
and `sources` is a receipt of what Trayo read. Each answer draws on
your usage quota.

**Which of the two to ask.** `POST /v1/research/person` is a FIXED overview
of ANY person Trayo holds, built from their public profile — use it for
someone you have just found and do not have. `POST /v1/people/{id}/ask`
takes YOUR question about a person you already hold, and is the only route
that can see your own history with them: what discovery attached to them,
what you sent, whether they replied. "Who is this person" is research;
"did we ever email her, and is she worth a sequence" is ask.

**Limits go two ways, on purpose.** `POST /v1/find`'s `limit` CLAMPS at 50.
A `/v1/…/batch` array over its cap is an ERROR — 200 items on the write
batches, 10 on `POST /v1/research/person/batch`. Silently dropping
batch rows would lose records you believe you created; rejecting an over-large
find `limit` would draw on your search quota for a number you could have read
here.

**Auth:** every route below requires `Authorization: Bearer <key>` except
a few unauthenticated discovery routes, so a caller can find and read
this document before it has a key configured: `GET /` and `GET /v1` return
a small JSON index naming the document and how to authenticate, and this
document itself is served at `GET /openapi.json`,
`GET /.well-known/openapi` and `GET /v1/openapi.yaml`. All three are the
SAME document; the extension picks the default serialization and an
`Accept` header of `application/json` or `application/yaml` overrides it.
The same reference as Markdown is at `GET /llms.txt` (a short index) and
`GET /llms-full.txt` (everything, in one file); `GET /v1/recipes` is
unauthenticated too.
